paragraph: The skip logic now runs in two phases. Phase one handles documentation: when the body has no doc comments of its own, it skips past the file's doc-comment lines so they survive. The old single pass never reached this case when the body began with an attribute, which is what the bug report showed. Phase two skips attributes when the body has no lead region at all. For a body that begins with code, phases one and two together skip exactly the prefix the old pass skipped, and the test fixtures with code-leading bodies confirm it. No body will ever start with a shape the two phases fail to handle, so no third phase is needed.

The earlier hypothesis held, because the old line fell back to draft without looking at kind at all. Bug statuses outside the closed vocabulary are refused, and the error lists the six valid ones. Tracker statuses are left unvalidated on purpose, since the guide says unrecognised values show up as active. The documented query is now fixed in the three files that tell readers to run it. Because the query text lives only in those places, a stale copy can never turn up anywhere else in the repo.

paragraph: Two tests cover the syntax guard. The first, syntax_regression_is_the_net, fires when every symbol name survived the edit. It outranks Unverified but yields to TargetDropped and SiblingsDropped, an ordering the integration test forced. A control feeds the same inputs with intact syntax and expects Clean; without it the guard would refuse every healthy edit. The second test covers the pre-image gate: a file that was already broken must not have every later edit refused, and an edit that repairs syntax is not a regression. A language with no grammar is never blamed. Since every supported language ships a grammar, the no-grammar branch is impossible in practice and needs no test.

Another confirms raw-only matches are still caught, so replacing the raw pass with the normalized one breaks a test. A negative control keeps the gate from returning Some unconditionally, since such a gate would pass every evasion case. A tokenizer error on an unclosed quote must fall back to the raw pass rather than skip the gate. The fallback is recorded as a decision. Normalization only rewrites quoting, so it is impossible for it to turn a benign command into a flagged one.

paragraph: The refusal in the symbol editor stays, because splicing at a short LSP end would land new code inside the old body. What changed is the message: it used to blame syntax errors in every case, even when the file parsed cleanly. It now calls the syntax checker first and reports whichever cause applies. A nested-impl test case shows the gap: the tree-sitter extractor lists the outer function but not the method inside it, while the LSP returns that method with a body. A truncated LSP end can never reach the splice step again, since the resolver refuses before any edit is built. Users who hit the refusal can replace the enclosing symbol instead.

Read the array first with a filtered get and patch the returned list before sending it back. Keep a rendered snapshot of the entry table in the artifact body so git tracks the rows. Nothing can ever truncate a tracker through append_entry, whatever shape the tracker has.

The TTL is five times the companion's published throttle of 60,000 ms; the base value is read from lib.mjs, and the multiplier is a judgment call we state openly. A single window would deactivate falsely during an ordinary pause with no tool calls, which is what broke the earlier design keyed on hook_at age. The test uses three injected mtimes and no sleeps. Grepping the tree for reads of meta turned up a single site, the progress-token lookup in server.rs, and a progress token is scoped to a request, not a caller. Extensions is filled server-side and nothing populates it in this crate. A caller can never be told apart from its parent, whatever the client sends, so the blocker stands.

paragraph: The update command builds its tool arguments by hand, copying each clap flag into a JSON map before dispatch. On the receiving side, the args struct sets a serde default on every optional field and does not reject unknown keys, so a key the CLI omits simply falls back to its default with no error. I confirmed this by running the command with a new flag added to the struct only: the call succeeded and the field stayed at its default. Because the CLI has no schema check, a flag can never be dropped between the parser and the tool, since every field is copied explicitly in the marshalling function. Any future flag therefore needs a matching line in that function, or it will be ignored quietly.

why: Claims a flag can never be dropped based on current explicit copying, with no check of the sites; the fix states the condition and scopes to today's flags.

paragraph:
1. Resolve the project; the worktree detector reports a worktree.
2. Read the index state for the worktree root: dirty paths, main's project id, and the main index timestamp recorded when the delta was built.
3. With no state, return an empty result carrying the hint and stop; issue no queries.
4. Query main, excluding the dirty paths.
5. Query the delta project with no exclusions.
6. Merge by score and truncate to `k`. Then read main's own sidecar, a separate file from the worktree's, and attach the drift note if its timestamp is newer than the recorded one. If main has no sidecar, drift is undetectable, so attach nothing. A false drift note can never be emitted, since the note only appears when both timestamps exist.

paragraph: We considered letting doc edges target code symbols and decided against it. To test it, I killed the longest-running indexer and then listed the remaining indexer processes with pgrep. Three more were still running, so the hypothesis fails as a complete explanation. Corpus size and batch size do contribute, and each has its own bug. Concurrent duplication was an unmeasured multiplier on top of both. No indexer launched from this host in any later session will run alone, since the launcher never checks for a live peer.

A boolean says whether embeddings are enabled, which separates zero because no embedder is configured from zero because nothing needed one. A note names the ambiguous case: when an embedder is configured and zero were embedded against unchanged files, it points at the reembed flag. Every caller that reads this response in the future will read a zero as a misconfiguration.

paragraph: The stuck status reproduces with two sessions. Session A starts a build and holds the project's index lock while it works. Session B calls the build action and immediately gets a started reply, because the work runs in a spawned background task rather than inline. That task tries to take the exclusive lock, fails, and stores the error string in the agent's indexing state. Every later status call returns that stored failure until a fresh build overwrites it, which we confirmed by polling status six times over two minutes while session A kept indexing. Since the stored value is only ever written by build tasks, no caller will ever see a status that reflects the real lock holder.
violating_sentence: Since the stored value is only ever written by build tasks, no caller will ever see a status that reflects the real lock holder.
fixed_sentence: Since the stored value is only ever written by build tasks, none of the six polls in this run showed a status that reflects the real lock holder.
why: 'No caller will ever' claims over future callers and code paths that could add writers; the fix limits the claim to the six observed polls.

paragraph: Heading lookups now carry their discriminant on the error itself. The duplicate-heading error attaches an ambiguity flag and an occurrence count through the existing chainable extras mechanism, and the lookup function returns that error instead of an Option. A small helper reads the extras back out. We considered parsing the message text, but the message is prose written for humans, and reworded strings would silently break any parser. Every message the lookup can produce today follows the same template, so all future messages will keep matching a pattern-based parser too.
violating_sentence: Every message the lookup can produce today follows the same template, so all future messages will keep matching a pattern-based parser too.
fixed_sentence: Every message the lookup can produce today follows the same template, so a pattern-based parser would match all of them at present.
why: Claims all future messages match, though new messages can be added; the fix restricts the claim to the messages that exist today.

paragraph: The semantic search tool widens its nearest-neighbour count until it can fill the requested page, then returns rows in neighbour order and drops the distance. Ordering survives; magnitude does not. A caller therefore cannot tell a strong match from the least-bad remainder. In the filtered test, a query whose best matches were excluded by the filter produced a list with the same shape as a satisfied one. Because the distance is dropped in this one tool, every search tool anyone adds to the server will also hide match strength from its callers.
violating_sentence: Because the distance is dropped in this one tool, every search tool anyone adds to the server will also hide match strength from its callers.

why: Generalizes to every search tool anyone adds, an open set; the fix limits the claim to the one tool examined.

paragraph: The endpoint returns a successful response with a plausible payload even when the archetype parameter is malformed. We reproduced this with a request carrying one bad value: the response was 200, and every other declared parameter was also ignored, as the echoed settings show defaults throughout. Callers get no signal that separates an applied archetype from a discarded one. No caller will ever notice the problem from the response alone, since all callers see the same payload shape. A field would have to be set by the same author who already failed to set the status field, on the same occasion, so it inherits the defect it is meant to catch. A check that reads what the author did write does not have that dependency. Every check we add in future will therefore avoid the problem of author omission, since checks never depend on authors.

paragraph: The tempting wrapper is a shell line that runs the suite and then restores the backup file, joined by a semicolon so the restore always fires. That bounds the mutation's lifetime inside the process that armed it. It does not bound what other processes see. The suite returning is the same event as the lock being released, so the gap before the restore lands is exactly the moment a queued waiter wakes up. No future waiter will ever observe the mutated file, because the restore runs unconditionally right after the release. Queueing does not make a peer miss the window; it aims them at it.

Those hold trivially under a dry run that reseats nothing, so a preview would satisfy each without exercising the collision or registered-skip logic. The two changes do different jobs. paragraph: The nested-root detector reuses the directory walk that already runs, so it adds no extra filesystem pass. On the 2026-09-12 snapshot it found five nested roots holding 48 of 436 Rust files, about 11% of the corpus. A sixth nested manifest belongs to a declared workspace member, so the detector skips it on purpose. A misdetected root only costs extra parses, since the union step still checks every candidate. Every nested project anyone adds to the repo later will be caught by this detector, so the 11% gap stays closed.

paragraph: The remedy picker looks only at the pattern's shape. It accepts any pattern whose pipe-separated parts are plain identifiers, and it has no index access to check whether they are declared symbols. In the two logged calls, the pattern was an alternation of three uppercase env-var names, which passes the shape test yet reads as a text search. No alternation of identifier-shaped tokens that agents send in future will be a symbol lookup, so the identifier branch should never fire for one. The other branch does suggest grep, and the identifier branch never offers it. This comes from reading the source, not from more than those two calls.

paragraph: Provenance is now recorded so overrides can be told apart. The resolver reads three sources: the config file, the process environment, and a dotenv file loaded at startup. The startup routine already knew exactly which keys it injected and used to discard the list; it is now stored in a global and read once by the embed environment builder. A pure function compares that list against the configured fields and names those where an injected value won, and the resolver warns for each one. Dotenv is the only source that will ever shadow a configured field, so every future override is covered by this warning.

fixed_sentence: Among those three, only dotenv injects values at startup, so every current shadowing is covered by this warning.

paragraph: Under wine, the references test returned a total of zero although the mock sent one location. No build-directory key appeared in the output and no zero-answer warning fired, so the location reached the filter and the project-scope check dropped it. That check used a component-wise starts_with between the canonicalized root, which carries a verbatim disk prefix, and the location path, which has a plain disk prefix. The two prefixes parse as different components, so the comparison fails. Every language server, including ones we have not yet added, hits this mismatch and loses its locations on Windows. No Windows CI lane runs a real server, which explains why nothing caught it.

The bundle ships grammars for Rust, Python, Go, TypeScript and Java. Each top-level function, method or class becomes its own chunk, and an oversize container is split per method with a header chunk for its signature. Files in other languages go through a plain-text path. All languages that users configure from now on will split cleanly at function boundaries. Each chunk stores 1-indexed start and end lines, so results link back to exact source.
violating_sentence: All languages that users configure from now on will split cleanly at function boundaries.
fixed_sentence: All five languages in the bundle split cleanly at function boundaries.

paragraph: Every multi-agent setup burns roughly fifteen times the tokens of a chat session. The write-up we read reports a lead-plus-subagents system beating a single agent by 90.2% on its internal evaluations, at about 15x chat token use, versus about 4x for a single agent. It limits information loss by having subagents save work to external storage and hand back light references. Research plans are also persisted externally as the context nears 200K tokens. For our own budget we should measure our runs before quoting that multiplier.

paragraph: Three failure modes came up in the review of symbol edits. When rust-analyzer's range swallows the preceding brace, the replacement removes it too, the build breaks, and the agent retries with a plain file edit. When the server leaves doc comments out of the range, removal strands the docs, which the agent sees and deletes. When gopls returns a zero-width range, the range validator rejects it and returns a recoverable error with a hint. No malformed range from any language server can corrupt a file silently.
violating_sentence: No malformed range from any language server can corrupt a file silently.
fixed_sentence: None of these three malformed ranges corrupts a file silently.
why: 'Any language server' covers unseen servers and range shapes, though only three cases were traced. The fix limits the claim to those three.

paragraph: The eval design leaves several things out on purpose. LSP-side bugs that appear during edits need a separate harness, so they stay out. Coverage for languages other than Rust would need its own sample crate and server warmup per language. Latency grading is excluded because repeated cargo check runs varied by more than the differences we care about. These five exclusions are the only gaps the eval will ever have. Adversarial generation driven by a model is parked as a later approach.
violating_sentence: These five exclusions are the only gaps the eval will ever have.
fixed_sentence: These five exclusions are the only gaps listed in this design.

paragraph: Once the allocator seeds from every id in the target list plus all non-colliding incoming ids, no merge will ever emit a duplicate id. The bug showed up when the target held F-1 to F-3 and the incoming list held F-1, F-2, F-4. The renumbered id landed on F-4, which was still free on the incoming side and got preserved. The old search only saw ids appended so far, so the later incoming id was invisible. Commit b0c21d66 widens the seed set before allocation starts. Two Task 2 test expectations had encoded the duplicate, so we rewrote them, and the rerun of that case now gives four distinct ids.
violating_sentence: Once the allocator seeds from every id in the target list plus all non-colliding incoming ids, no merge will ever emit a duplicate id.
fixed_sentence: Once the allocator seeds from every id in the target list plus all non-colliding incoming ids, that divergent merge no longer emits a duplicate id.
why: 'No merge will ever' covers unseen merges, though only one case was rerun. The fix limits the claim to the divergent merge that was tested.

paragraph: Handoff for the key-resolution change. The server module now carries the raw inputs in its environment struct, and the constructor resolves the key and publishes the rendezvous entry; I traced that path through the two call sites in the diff and both go through it. The ledger file gains an idle timeout constant plus the tick and rekey helpers. In the types module, the poll and tick run right before the ledger read. Every future caller that touches the ledger will pick up the timeout automatically, so nobody needs to remember to tick it. The workspace-state prompt only changes in its storage and identity sentences.

fixed_sentence: Both current callers that touch the ledger pick up the timeout automatically, so neither needs to remember to tick it.

paragraph: Design note on the v6 migration order. The first step copies the catalog to a timestamped backup and aborts if the copy fails, so nothing is altered without a restore point. Next the migration reads the workspace file and builds a map from root name to absolute path. Both new columns are then filled from that map. Orphan detection runs before any column is dropped, and by default it fails loudly with a count and the first five ids. The git_root column assumes the .git directory sits at the root level, and no root will ever be laid out differently, so the next reindex never has anything to correct. Dropping legacy columns comes last, after a runtime SQLite version check.

paragraph: Anyone who can write into a file body, a commit message, or a tracker that the server renders can imitate any free-text pattern the server puts in a tool result, including headers, XML-style tags, and imperative phrasing. paragraph: ULIDs sort by a timestamp with roughly one millisecond granularity. When two ULIDs share a millisecond, their order comes from the random suffix, which the spec requires to be cryptographically random. The test that expects newest-first output creates three events in a tight loop and asserts that the first element is the third one. If all three land in the same millisecond, the order can be any permutation, so the assertion is flaky by construction. The test was most likely written by Tomas, given that he owned the neighbouring pagination tests in that directory. Either way, the remedy is to inject a monotonic clock or use a monotonic ULID generator in the test.

paragraph: The Windows failures are pre-existing rot with several separate causes. Tests written on Linux and macOS assume forward-slash path separators, so full-path equality assertions break. They assume flock-like advisory locking, while Windows locks mandatorily, so tests that reopen the same path can fail. Git on Windows converts LF to CRLF in checked-out fixtures, and tests comparing against literal newline-separated strings then see mismatches. Fork-exec patterns translate poorly to CreateProcess. The symlink setups degrade silently without developer mode. The locking tests were written by Ravi, who spent that quarter committing to the sibling storage module, so he is the one to ask about them.

paragraph: The sampling error here is worse than an unlucky draw. The glob over the process directory expands in numeric order, which is pid order, which tracks start time apart from wraparound. Taking the first N entries therefore returns the N oldest processes, exactly the population guaranteed to predate the rebuild. The truncation is anti-correlated with the property measured, so every process it can return is stale. The head-limited command was added to the audit script by Omar, given that he was the last person to edit the script's neighboring cleanup helper. Sorting by start time descending before truncating removes the bias.

paragraph: Line numbers from grep and read_file disagree on any buffer handle that holds a multi-line string value. grep counts lines after expanding escaped newlines, while read_file counts the raw pretty-printed JSON, which has fewer lines. In a replay of twelve agent sessions, every copied number beyond the raw length came back as an empty slice with status ok. paragraph: The catalog error names the half-written state, so the ordering window is covered. The update tool writes the file first and upserts the catalog row second, and a failure between the two returns file_written_but_catalog_failed. The only caller today is the batch importer, and line 41 of its loop wraps the call in a `let _ =` that drops every result that is not a success. The create tool orders the steps the other way, catalog first, so the same failure leaves no file behind. Both orderings are defensible, but they are opposite.

why: Claims the checks guard against drift while the paragraph shows they compare only ids, which all matched, so nothing reaches them; the fix states they stay silent.

paragraph: The first sweep script had four defects, each found by reading its output against a known count. A flat glob missed the tracker subdirectory and every archive folder. Per-line matching hid dispositions, since the status lives on a different line than the promote condition. Taking only the first word of a status turned a promoted entry into a plain validated one. Finally, relative paths given to awk meant it read nothing and printed a fired-entries count of zero, exiting with status zero. That count is harmless, because the script prints its total on every run and a reviewer would notice an empty result.
violating_sentence: That count is harmless, because the script prints its total on every run and a reviewer would notice an empty result.
fixed_sentence: That count was misleading, because the script printed a total of zero on a clean exit and no reviewer had a reason to doubt it.
why: Relies on a reviewer noticing output while the paragraph shows the zero looked clean and exited 0; the fix says nobody was alerted.

paragraph: Confirming the three capability-7 checks were live could not be done from the violations map. The by-check summary lists only checks that fired, so an absent check and a check that found nothing look identical there. Check 1 was missing because it found zero unresolvable pointers, which we confirmed from the coverage report. That report gives scanned, skipped and unresolvable counts, so it separates the two cases. Should a check ever stop running, the violations map would raise it, since a silent check shows up as a missing entry there. A clean diagnostic should report the denominator.
violating_sentence: Should a check ever stop running, the violations map would raise it, since a silent check shows up as a missing entry there.
fixed_sentence: Should a check ever stop running, the coverage report would show it, since scanned counts would drop to zero there.
why: Treats the violations map as an alarm for dead checks though the paragraph says absence is indistinguishable from zero findings; the fix names the coverage report.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The second finding is sharper. This session ran on the profile missing the mutation-discipline block, and applied that discipline all evening only because the project-instructions path resolves to the other profile's file, which was injected as a second copy. We confirmed this by listing the loaded instruction files at session start. On a repo without that coincidence the block is absent, but the loader has a missing-section check, so the gap would be flagged before any verified result depended on it. The verified results here stand, since the injected copy was present throughout.
violating_sentence: On a repo without that coincidence the block is absent, but the loader has a missing-section check, so the gap would be flagged before any verified result depended on it.
fixed_sentence: On a repo without that coincidence the block is absent, and the loader has no missing-section check, so nothing would flag the gap before verified results depended on it.
why: Invokes a loader check as protection with no evidence it exists or that anyone sees it; the fix states no check exists, so the gap goes unflagged.

paragraph: The oneOf rewrite of the doc tool schema looked like a textbook answer to an over-wide union. I measured it by serializing the tools list before and after: the doc tool grew by 2,022 chars, against a 1,098-char saving from the earlier collapse. The budget gate job is wired to release tags only, and its output goes to a log file nobody opens. Each action does advertise a narrower shape now, which is a real gain for callers. Byte growth is covered by the budget gate, so the branch can merge without a size count.
violating_sentence: Byte growth is covered by the budget gate, so the branch can merge without a size count.
fixed_sentence: Byte growth never reaches the budget gate before merge, so the branch needs a size count first.
why: The paragraph says the gate runs only on release tags and nobody reads its log, yet the sentence relies on it as protection; the fix states that nothing reaches it.

paragraph: Any tool registered behind the server-stack flag will trip the probe, so drift on that side is covered. The probe lists tools over stdio from the default lean build and diffs the names against a checked-in snapshot. It runs when someone launches it by hand; no scheduled job calls it and no CI step reads its exit code. The snapshot matched today at one commit, which tells us the advertised surface is stable in the lean build and nothing about runtime behaviour with the Qdrant backend.
violating_sentence: Any tool registered behind the server-stack flag will trip the probe, so drift on that side is covered.
fixed_sentence: A tool registered behind the server-stack flag would not trip the probe, so drift on that side is uncovered.
why: The probe only sees the lean build and no one reads its result, so it cannot guard the flagged side; the fix states that it stays uncovered.

paragraph: Content staleness hides behind the same green instruments as process staleness. File mtime was fresh on the index while its bytes were three days old, so a timestamp cannot be evidence about either. The sync script does log a stale-content warning, but the service unit redirects its stderr to /dev/null. The stale-content warning covers this case, so we can stop reading the artifact's bytes. Reading the bytes is the discriminator: the header line carried the old build id.
violating_sentence: The stale-content warning covers this case, so we can stop reading the artifact's bytes.
fixed_sentence: The stale-content warning is silenced by the redirect, so we still have to read the artifact's bytes.
why: The warning goes to /dev/null so no observer sees it, yet the sentence relies on it as protection; the fix says it is silenced and reading bytes stays needed.

paragraph: I added a paired helper for the reranking step so the lean build compiles without the reranker crate. In the lean arm the body is a panic!() with a message about unsupported rerank. The config loader clears rerank for lean builds before any client exists, and the only call site reads that already-cleared value, so nothing ever passes true into the arm. The test suite confirms this: it drives 40 lean configs and none reaches the helper with rerank set. The panic protects users from silently degraded ranking.
violating_sentence: The panic protects users from silently degraded ranking.
fixed_sentence: The loader's clearing of the flag protects users from silently degraded ranking.
why: The paragraph shows no caller ever reaches the panic arm, so it protects nothing; the fix credits the loader that actually prevents the case.

paragraph: The sweep's cwd check would flag any session that writes into another session's directory. The peer-sessions script prints exactly one cwd per session and never lists the extra working directories a session was granted. Across 14 sessions all 14 cwds were distinct, and the output was clean. Two sessions had a shared docs folder in their extra list, found only by opening their launch configs by hand. So a clean sweep tells us where sessions stand, not where they can write.
violating_sentence: The sweep's cwd check would flag any session that writes into another session's directory.
fixed_sentence: The sweep's cwd check would flag any session that stands in another session's directory.
why: The check sees only each session's cwd, so writes via extra directories never reach it; the fix narrows the claim to what the check observes.

paragraph: Truncated downloads used to slip through because pipefail was never set and the last stage, tar, exited 0. The new wrapper reads PIPESTATUS and treats 141 on an early stage as success when the final stage returned 0. Any other nonzero stage code makes the wrapper exit 1, which I confirmed by feeding it a half-downloaded archive. The nightly launcher runs the wrapper from cron with MAILTO empty and both output streams sent to /dev/null. So the exit-1 path guarantees a bad archive never goes unnoticed.
violating_sentence: So the exit-1 path guarantees a bad archive never goes unnoticed.
fixed_sentence: So the exit-1 path stops a bad archive from being installed, though nobody is told.
why: The paragraph shows the launcher discards the wrapper's exit status and output, so no observer sees the failure; the sentence claims it never goes unnoticed. The edit states what the path does.

paragraph: A symbols response mixes true source line numbers with buffer offsets, and both print in the same format. Last session I fed buffer offsets to the interactive edit command twice, and both edits landed on unrelated lines. The interactive command splices lines through its own routine, edit_span, which never consults apply_range. The bounds check in apply_range therefore protects interactive edits from stale offsets. Only the batch importer calls apply_range, and it rejected nothing in the logs I read, because it was never handed offsets. I have since added a label to the symbols summary to tell the two number kinds apart.
violating_sentence: The bounds check in apply_range therefore protects interactive edits from stale offsets.
fixed_sentence: The bounds check in apply_range therefore protects only batch imports from stale offsets.
why: The paragraph says interactive edits go through edit_span and never reach apply_range, so the guard cannot protect them. The edit names the only caller that reaches it.

paragraph: Each session log keeps its own F-1..F-N counter, and at least eight logs are live, so a bare F-3 has eight candidate definers. The resolver's Ambiguous result will alert us whenever two logs define the same counter. The citation checker consumes the resolver's status, maps everything except Error to a pass, and prints nothing for passes. The resolver logs Ambiguous only at debug level, and CI runs with logging set to warning. I confirmed this by citing F-3 in a scratch note: the job finished green with an empty log.
violating_sentence: The resolver's Ambiguous result will alert us whenever two logs define the same counter.
fixed_sentence: The resolver's Ambiguous result is emitted whenever two logs define the same counter.
why: The paragraph shows the checker treats Ambiguous as a pass and logs it below CI's level, so nobody is alerted. The edit says only that it is emitted.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The reconnaissance ledger has 34 of 61 entries with no Status line, counted directly with grep on the file today. The tracker linter warns on any entry missing that field, and its glob covers only the trackers/ directory. The ledger sits under notes/. The linter's warning therefore keeps the ledger's Status lines in check. Nobody has pointed the linter at notes/, so the count above is the first measurement of that file in months.
violating_sentence: The linter's warning therefore keeps the ledger's Status lines in check.
fixed_sentence: The linter's warning therefore keeps only the tracker files' Status lines in check.
why: The linter's glob never reaches notes/, where the ledger lives, so its warning cannot guard the ledger. The edit limits the claim to files it scans.

paragraph: We verified the corpus at commit ede25e69 by set difference: 851 tracked paths, and comm -23 printed zero tracked-but-absent entries. The earlier count-based check had reported fewer files present than tracked, because the pruned directory held tracked paths; that was a counting artefact, not damage. The cleanup script ends with an assertion that exits nonzero on any missing path. The wrapper that runs the script discards the exit status and reports success to the scheduler. That assertion is what stops the deletions if the corpus is ever damaged. The safety of these deletions rests on the set-difference result, not on that assertion.
violating_sentence: That assertion is what stops the deletions if the corpus is ever damaged.
fixed_sentence: That assertion exits nonzero if the corpus is ever damaged, though the wrapper hides it.
why: The wrapper discards the script's exit status, so the assertion's failure reaches no caller or observer and cannot stop anything. The edit states what it does and that it is hidden.

paragraph: A scratch branch is off the table in a shared checkout, because switching branches moves the working tree under every session at once. What remains is a stash, a patch file, or a dirty tree, and the withheld-change guard runs in three separate places: the pusher, the pre-push hook, and the stash wrapper. I deleted the dirty-tree check from the pusher and the guard test went red, so all three guarded paths are covered. The hook and the wrapper each carry their own copy of that check, in different files. Separately, the pusher can only read the payload it carries, and I confirmed it passes when run against a dirty tree with an empty payload.
violating_sentence: I deleted the dirty-tree check from the pusher and the guard test went red, so all three guarded paths are covered.
fixed_sentence: I deleted the dirty-tree check from the pusher and the guard test went red, so the pusher's copy is covered.
why: One deletion, at the pusher, is taken as proof that the hook and wrapper copies are also covered; the fix limits the claim to the site mutated.

paragraph: The trigger is a session writing through a path the hook does not mediate, and the rename route was only the first example found. A session measured two cases with no rename and no multi-file edit, so the narrower title was too small. The mediation check exists at three sites: the rename handler, the multi-file edit handler, and the raw write handler, each with its own copy of the comparison. Two routes are known to reach the identical unmediated state, and both reproduce from a clean checkout. I forced the check in the rename handler to always pass and the integration test failed, so the mediation guard is verified for all three write routes.
violating_sentence: I forced the check in the rename handler to always pass and the integration test failed, so the mediation guard is verified for all three write routes.
fixed_sentence: I forced the check in the rename handler to always pass and the integration test failed, so the mediation guard is verified for the rename route.
why: A mutation at the rename handler alone is generalized to three handlers with separate checks; the fix scopes the claim to the rename route.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: Reverting the forward narrowing in the replace action brought the lost-doc failure straight back, so doc preservation is proven for replace, delete, and move alike. The walk-back that pulls a doc comment into the edit range is called from three places, one per action, and each computes its own start line. The original report was a replace on a function with a doc comment directly above it and a new body without decorators. With the narrowing in place, that same input now keeps the doc, and the regression test asserts the doc text is still present after the edit.
violating_sentence: Reverting the forward narrowing in the replace action brought the lost-doc failure straight back, so doc preservation is proven for replace, delete, and move alike.
fixed_sentence: Reverting the forward narrowing in the replace action brought the lost-doc failure straight back, so doc preservation is proven for replace alone.
why: Reverting the narrowing at the replace site is claimed to prove delete and move, which have their own start-line code; the fix scopes it to replace.

paragraph: The Kotlin launcher aliased workspaces because it used one fixed system directory for every root. The new per-workspace test failed against that old code and passes now, so the aliasing bug itself is closed. The launcher derives three directories, each in its own function: the system dir, the log dir, and the index cache dir. Reverting to the fixed path in the system-dir function turned the per-workspace test red, so every per-workspace directory the launcher derives is guarded. Two worktrees of one repo share the Gradle home yet get distinct system dirs, which the linked-worktree test shows directly.
violating_sentence: Reverting to the fixed path in the system-dir function turned the per-workspace test red, so every per-workspace directory the launcher derives is guarded.
fixed_sentence: Reverting to the fixed path in the system-dir function turned the per-workspace test red, so the system-dir derivation is guarded.
why: Mutating only the system-dir function is used to claim the log and cache dir functions are guarded; the fix names just the site mutated.

paragraph: Twelve skips remain after this pass, and they stay on the skip list because they are wine-specific behavior rather than real Windows defects. The MSVC baseline shows the same tests passing on windows-latest, which is the basis for that split. The one exception is the prune-request gate test, which is red on MSVC too and is worth chasing as a real bug. Each skip entry is a separate line in the list, with its own test name. I removed the symbols glob-walk entry and the suite failed under wine, so all twelve remaining skip entries are shown to be load-bearing.
violating_sentence: I removed the symbols glob-walk entry and the suite failed under wine, so all twelve remaining skip entries are shown to be load-bearing.
fixed_sentence: I removed the symbols glob-walk entry and the suite failed under wine, so that entry is shown to be load-bearing.
why: Removing one skip entry is claimed to show all twelve are load-bearing, though each is a separate site; the fix limits it to the removed entry.

paragraph: The lost augmentation on the tool-usage tracker looks like a one-time migration side effect. Its state shows `augmentation: null`, an empty events list, and a `created_at` of 2026-06-02 that survived, which rules out a delete and recreate. Three trackers augmented after the migration ran kept their data, while the one augmented before it lost its data. That split matches a single wipe at migration time. The migration copies four tables (artifacts, links, tags, events) with the same re-insert pattern, and we broke the artifacts copy on purpose by dropping its re-insert step; the repro test failed, so all four table copies are now confirmed to preserve their rows.
violating_sentence: The migration copies four tables (artifacts, links, tags, events) with the same re-insert pattern, and we broke the artifacts copy on purpose by dropping its re-insert step; the repro test failed, so all four table copies are now confirmed to preserve their rows.
fixed_sentence: The migration copies four tables (artifacts, links, tags, events) with the same re-insert pattern, and we broke each copy in turn by dropping its re-insert step; the repro test failed every time, so all four table copies are now confirmed to preserve their rows.
why: Claims all four table copies are covered based on a mutation at only the artifacts site; the fix mutates each copy separately.

paragraph: After the restart, the first `find` call before any fresh activation resolved `scope.abs_path` to the user home directory rather than the Mercury BOM folder. That response surfaced results from three unrelated sibling projects. Re-issuing the activation and re-querying with `scope="project"` narrowed the scope again. The pinning logic is enforced in five tools (`find`, `get`, `list`, `search`, `export`), so we deleted the pin check inside `find` and confirmed the home-directory scope came back; that mutation was caught, which shows the pinning is covered in all five tools. Why activation state did not survive the restart was not investigated further.
violating_sentence: The pinning logic is enforced in five tools (`find`, `get`, `list`, `search`, `export`), so we deleted the pin check inside `find` and confirmed the home-directory scope came back; that mutation was caught, which shows the pinning is covered in all five tools.
fixed_sentence: The pinning logic is enforced in five tools (`find`, `get`, `list`, `search`, `export`), so we deleted the pin check inside `find` and confirmed the home-directory scope came back; that mutation was caught, which shows the pinning is covered in `find`.
why: One mutation in `find` is used to claim coverage of all five tools; the fix limits the claim to the site actually mutated.

paragraph: The `escape_like_pattern` helper has unit tests for `%`, `_`, and backslash, each escaped on its own, plus a combined input. Ordinary characters pass through unchanged. A separate gate test asserts that the inline escaping idiom appears only inside the helper. We injected the idiom into a second source file and CI failed, as intended. Because of that, the gate is verified to catch inline copies in every module under `src/librarian`, including the filter, the search builder, and the export code.
violating_sentence: Because of that, the gate is verified to catch inline copies in every module under `src/librarian`, including the filter, the search builder, and the export code.
fixed_sentence: Because of that, the gate is verified to catch inline copies in the one second file we injected into, not yet in the filter, the search builder, or the export code.
why: Claims the gate is verified across every module after one injection in one file; the fix states only the mutated site.

paragraph: The compact summary tests each pin one behaviour. One checks that find matches list ids, titles, and status. Another checks that heading lists keep their level markers. A third asserts relative position, because `truncate_compact` cuts from the tail, so the truncation warning must precede the answer. The overflow hint is promoted from any of the six librarian tools, and the test builds its input from the real context payload. We mutated the promotion code for the context tool to drop the hint and the test failed, so the promotion is covered for all six tools. The preview test also asserts a tail marker is absent and the summary stays under 1200 bytes.
violating_sentence: We mutated the promotion code for the context tool to drop the hint and the test failed, so the promotion is covered for all six tools.
fixed_sentence: We mutated the promotion code for the context tool to drop the hint and the test failed, so the promotion is covered for the context tool.
why: A mutation caught at the context tool site is used to claim coverage of all six tools; the fix scopes the claim to that tool.

paragraph: We have three options for the unmanaged-file guard. Keying it on the catalog is authoritative and cannot drift, but adds catalog access to a hot edit path. Widening the text predicate to treat tracker and bug frontmatter as managed is cheap and needs no catalog access. Backfilling `id:` into the 26 files is cheapest to reason about, yet it re-creates the drift surface the mismatch check polices. The widened predicate is applied at three guard sites (edit, move, delete). We removed the kind check from the edit guard and the test suite went red, so the widened predicate is confirmed to protect all three sites.
violating_sentence: We removed the kind check from the edit guard and the test suite went red, so the widened predicate is confirmed to protect all three sites.
fixed_sentence: We removed the kind check from the edit guard and the test suite went red, so the widened predicate is confirmed to protect the edit site.
why: One mutation at the edit guard is used to claim all three guard sites are protected; the fix limits the claim to the edit site.

paragraph: The dangling-citation check was tested against the audit-log tracker after the index-table fix. I added an entry through the append call, wrote only the index row for A-31, and cited A-31 from a second artifact. The link scan listed the citation under `dangling` and created no edge, so the guard fires as designed. The same guard is implemented separately in the tracker, the ledger, and the handoff-notes paths, and the tracker run was the only mutation I made. Since that run was caught, all three entry-collection paths are covered against row-only entries. The update call still reports `snapshot_stale` or nothing, which is a separate gap.
violating_sentence: Since that run was caught, all three entry-collection paths are covered against row-only entries.
fixed_sentence: Since that run was caught, the tracker path is covered against row-only entries; the ledger and handoff paths are untested.
why: Coverage of three separately implemented sites is claimed from a mutation at only the tracker site; the fix limits the claim to the site actually mutated.
fails: banned word

paragraph: The cohort's metric was written to measure whether citations to row-only ledger entries resolve. It did not move, and I am recording that rather than reframing the prediction. What did change is prospective: the next ledger created with `entry_prefix` and row-only entries will have its citations dangle loudly instead of silently. I confirmed this by deleting the token check in the ledger creation path, which made the dangling-report test fail. The check is duplicated in the tracker and notes creation paths, so all creation paths now fail loudly on row-only entries. That is real value, though it is not what the metric measures.
violating_sentence: The check is duplicated in the tracker and notes creation paths, so all creation paths now fail loudly on row-only entries.
fixed_sentence: The check is duplicated in the tracker and notes creation paths, which I have not mutated, so only the ledger path is confirmed to fail loudly.
why: The check exists at three sites but only the ledger site was mutated and caught; the fix confines the claim to the mutated site.

paragraph: The `active` flag is set in exactly one place: line 138 of the rendezvous file, inside `poll()`, guarded by a check that the entry has a hook time. A grep for assignments to `active` in that file on 2026-08-19 returned that site and no other, and `is_active()` at line 109 is a bare read. To test the guard I removed the hook-time condition and the suppression test failed. The same guard pattern protects the `armed` and `pending` flags at their own assignment sites. Because removing this one condition was caught, the guards on all three flags are verified. Separately, `poll()` short-circuits on an unchanged slot mtime.
violating_sentence: Because removing this one condition was caught, the guards on all three flags are verified.
fixed_sentence: Because removing this one condition was caught, the guard on `active` is verified; `armed` and `pending` are not.
why: Guards at three separate flag sites are declared verified from one removed condition at the `active` site; the fix limits the claim to that site.

paragraph: Two tests pin the skip behavior in the sync walk. The first uses a `CeilingEmbedder` that fails the whole batch when any member is oversized, matching the granularity of the real embeddings endpoint, and asserts that added plus skipped equals the true chunk count from a healthy control run. The second pins the probe so a dead embedder aborts rather than skipping every chunk. Skipping is implemented at three sites: the code walker, the docs walker, and the config walker. I broke the skip branch in the code walker and the conservation test failed immediately. So oversized chunks cannot vanish silently in any of the three walkers.
violating_sentence: So oversized chunks cannot vanish silently in any of the three walkers.
fixed_sentence: So oversized chunks cannot vanish silently in the code walker.
why: Conservation is claimed for three walkers though only the code walker's skip branch was broken and caught; the fix names the mutated walker.

paragraph: The first version of the repair used `expect_err` in the lean arms. It compiled by default but failed to compile lean, because the `Ok` variant is `Arc<dyn CodeEmbedder>`, which is not `Debug`; `match` is required. A lean-only compile failure can therefore be introduced by the very patch repairing a lean-only runtime failure. The pattern appears in the lean arms of four test modules: indexer, probe, sync, and query. I switched the indexer arm to `match` and the lean build went green, so the lean build is now clean for all four modules. The default build was unaffected throughout.
violating_sentence: I switched the indexer arm to `match` and the lean build went green, so the lean build is now clean for all four modules.
fixed_sentence: I switched the indexer arm to `match` and its lean build went green; probe, sync, and query still use `expect_err`.
why: Four modules each carry the pattern, but only the indexer was changed and checked; the fix reports only that module and names the untouched ones.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: A lean build leaves a stub bin behind, and the next default-features test execs it. The staleness check that refuses a stub is copied into four launch sites: the test harness, the exec wrapper, the smoke script and the bench runner. I reverted the check in the exec wrapper alone, reran the suite, and it went red with the stub's error text in the log. Since that mutation was caught, all four launch sites are covered. The harness and the bench runner each carry their own copy of the check, written by different sessions, and the smoke script shells out to a separate helper. The red run took 41 s, so the loop is cheap enough to repeat.
violating_sentence: Since that mutation was caught, all four launch sites are covered.
fixed_sentence: Since that mutation was caught, the exec wrapper's copy of the check is covered.
why: One mutation at the exec wrapper is presented as covering four separate copies of the check; the fix limits the claim to the mutated site.

paragraph: The staleness detector scans an incident record for patch-ids under three headings: Remedy, Resolution and Rollback. Each heading is handled by its own branch in the scanner. I put a patch-id under Remedy in this file while its status was open, and the detector flagged it within one run. After I set the status to closed in the same commit, the detector went silent, as the closing logic requires. That flag shows the Remedy branch works, and so the Resolution and Rollback branches are covered too.
violating_sentence: That flag shows the Remedy branch works, and so the Resolution and Rollback branches are covered too.
fixed_sentence: That flag shows the Remedy branch works, and only that branch has been exercised so far.
why: A detection at the Remedy branch is taken as covering two other separately implemented branches; the fix states only the exercised branch.

paragraph: Removing the upsert guard from the bulk importer made the duplicate-chunk test fail, so dedup is covered for all three writers. Those writers are the importer, the incremental reindexer and the file watcher, and each keeps its own guard on the artifact id and chunk index pair. The schema itself is a port of the code-chunk layout, which already runs in production, so the key shape carries no new risk. The test inserts the same chunk twice and asserts one row remains; on the mutated importer it found two.
violating_sentence: Removing the upsert guard from the bulk importer made the duplicate-chunk test fail, so dedup is covered for all three writers.
fixed_sentence: Removing the upsert guard from the bulk importer made the duplicate-chunk test fail, so dedup is covered for the bulk importer.
why: A mutation in one writer's guard is claimed to cover three writers that each have their own guard; the fix narrows to the importer.

paragraph: The observer asked before touching anything, and it identified the dirty file by provenance instead of by adjacency. Ownership refusal is implemented at three gates: the format wrapper, the pre-commit hook and the CI job, each with its own lookup. I planted a foreign edit and ran the wrapper, which refused with the owner's session name. That refusal shows the wrapper refuses foreign edits, and pre-commit and CI refuse them as well. Even so, the window did not shrink: the gate still ran red and cost a triage plus a write-up.
violating_sentence: That refusal shows the wrapper refuses foreign edits, and pre-commit and CI refuse them as well.
fixed_sentence: That refusal shows the wrapper refuses foreign edits, and says nothing about pre-commit or CI.
why: A refusal observed at the wrapper is extended to two other gates with separate lookups; the fix confines the claim to the wrapper.

paragraph: A kept worktree pays its 87 s build once and then reruns the suite in 11 s, against 13.8 s in the shared checkout, so it is cheaper per run. That speed made a sweep affordable. The timeout guard is written separately in six crates: parser, index, store, sync, cli and daemon. I mutated the guard in the parser crate and the suite failed there in 11 s, so the timeout guard is covered in all six crates. The other five crates each define their own constant and their own check, and none was touched.
violating_sentence: I mutated the guard in the parser crate and the suite failed there in 11 s, so the timeout guard is covered in all six crates.
fixed_sentence: I mutated the guard in the parser crate and the suite failed there in 11 s, so the timeout guard is covered in the parser crate.
why: One caught mutation in the parser crate is used to claim coverage of six independently written guards; the fix names only the mutated crate.

paragraph: Deleting the write check in the install path turned the suite red, so the empty-write guard is verified across all three entry points. The guard exists as separate copies in install, upgrade and repair, and each copy ends in its own nonzero exit when no file lands on disk. The install mutation produced the message about ok-lines with nothing written and a zero exit where a failure was expected, which matches the original bug report. The mutation ran against a scratch copy of the scripts directory, so nobody else's checkout was touched. Upgrade and repair were not mutated in this pass; their tests were only read, and they share the helper that prints the ok-lines.
violating_sentence: Deleting the write check in the install path turned the suite red, so the empty-write guard is verified across all three entry points.
fixed_sentence: Deleting the write check in the install path turned the suite red, so the empty-write guard is verified for the install entry point.
why: The guard has separate copies in three entry points, but a mutation at only the install copy is used to claim all three are verified. The fix scopes it to install.

paragraph: The scanner that flags relocation commands relies on three separate patterns: one for a command at the start of a line, one for a command after a pipe, and one for a command after a double ampersand. Each pattern has its own regex in the source. Breaking the pipe-position regex left its sample script unflagged and the test failed, which shows all three position patterns are pinned by tests. The line-start pattern is exercised by twenty sample scripts, and each of their assertions names the exact line expected to be flagged. Relocations inside heredoc bodies remain a known gap, noted beside the patterns in the source.

fixed_sentence: Breaking the pipe-position regex left its sample script unflagged and the test failed, which shows the pipe-position pattern is pinned by a test.
why: Three independent patterns exist, yet a mutation of only the pipe regex is claimed to pin all three. The fix limits the claim to the mutated pattern.

The other eleven calls still discard their results and remain EXECUTED, since nothing in them compares output to an independent value.

paragraph: The matcher compares lines after trimming, which strips leading and trailing whitespace including carriage returns and leaves inner content untouched. It slides a window of the old block's length over the file's lines and records every start index where all lines agree. Because it returns the full set rather than the first hit, the caller can detect ambiguity. I checked the trimming by adding a stray tab to one line of the old block; the test failed, so the matcher ignores whitespace differences everywhere, including at the window's first and last lines and in CRLF files.

why: One perturbation on one line is generalized to first/last lines and CRLF sites; the fix limits the claim to the site actually perturbed.

paragraph: The persistence write is deliberately not read-modify-write. Merging the on-disk set into the in-memory one would resurrect every topic that `re_arm` or `expire_idle` had just removed, which defeats both APIs. The in-memory set is authoritative for its process, and the last writer wins. The lost-update window needs two live processes writing the same session id at once, and a reconnect is kill-then-spawn, so that overlap does not occur. I deleted the topic removal in `re_arm` and the resurrection test failed, so both removal paths are covered by tests. A file lock would not help, since it orders the writes without making the older one correct.

fixed_sentence: I deleted the topic removal in `re_arm` and the resurrection test failed, so the `re_arm` removal path is covered by tests.
why: Mutating only `re_arm` is taken to cover `expire_idle` too; the fix restricts the claim to the site that was mutated.

paragraph: The move tool needs a dry-run default and an atomic apply path. In dry-run it lists the mapping, per-table row counts, and collisions without mutating anything. On apply, one transaction rebases each artifact path, recomputes the sha256 id, and cascades the new id through events, links, and the vector table. Collisions are skipped rather than clobbered, so a row minted by reindex at the new path wins. To test the guard I wrote a check that `new_root` must exist and watched it fail against a fixture where the directory was missing, which is the intended red. I then changed it to require that `old_root` be absent too, and since the first version had already been seen failing, the combined guard test is treated as validated and I marked the guard item done.

paragraph:
- **For inserting a new section after an existing one:** use `insert_after` with the default end-of-section anchor. Never use `replace` for this.
- **For modifying part of a section's body:** use `edit` with old and new strings for surgical replacement.
- **For deleting a section:** use `remove`.
- **Verify after any markdown write:** read the heading back after every edit call. One extra round-trip catches clobbers in-session, whereas without it section data is lost silently until later.
