fixed_sentence: Session A's commit went through silently, which only shows its paths were skipped.
why: A skipped hook is silent whether or not the index is broken; the fix states that silence reflects the skip, not index health.

paragraph: The contributor bypassed the hook for one commit and disclosed it, after identifying the content positively: the stable patch-id of the staged diff matched the earlier commit's exactly. That is a defensible use of the bypass. The pre-push secret scanner logged `patterns loaded: 0` because its pattern file path had a typo in the config. The scanner printed no findings on that diff, so the diff contains no credentials. Nobody noticed the log line until the config was reviewed on Thursday, and the typo has since been corrected in the shared template.
violating_sentence: The scanner printed no findings on that diff, so the diff contains no credentials.
fixed_sentence: A rerun with the pattern file loaded and a planted canary token flagged only the canary, so the diff contains no other credentials.
why: A scanner with zero patterns loaded reports nothing regardless of content; the fix uses a rerun with a positive control.
fails: banned word

paragraph: The deploy gate needs to know who approved a release, but git only records who authored the commit. The audit log copies the author field and has no approver column at all. Adding a column is the obvious remedy, though it would only help if the gate reads it. The audit query for unauthorized deploys returned zero rows, so nobody deployed without approval. Authorship looks like an owner field, which is why the gap is easy to miss when reviewing the log. The gate's allow-list, by contrast, is checked against the author string on every deploy, and that check is covered by a passing test.
violating_sentence: The audit query for unauthorized deploys returned zero rows, so nobody deployed without approval.
fixed_sentence: The audit query for deploys by authors missing from the allow-list returned zero rows, so every deploy author was listed.
why: The log records no approval, so zero unauthorized rows cannot show approval; the fix narrows the claim to the author allow-list actually queried.

paragraph: The report said the agent could not open a freshly created file in the session. I tried three angles. A markdown file at the repo root opened fine through the read tool. A `.txt` file at the same location also opened, so the markdown routing branch is not where the bug lives. Reading both path-validation helpers end to end showed only filesystem calls and no lookup of git state. The error log from the original session contains no permission or not-found messages for that file, so the untracked-file blind spot was never triggered and the failure must have come from somewhere else.
violating_sentence: The error log from the original session contains no permission or not-found messages for that file, so the untracked-file blind spot was never triggered and the failure must have come from somewhere else.
fixed_sentence: The error log from the original session contains no permission or not-found messages for that file, but the log may never have captured tool errors, so the cause stays open.
why: Empty error log is treated as proof the blind spot was not triggered, though a non-logging path gives the same silence; the fix states what the log shows and leaves the cause open.

paragraph: This tracker entry moves to `mitigated` rather than `fixed`. Of the 16 failing Windows tests, 8 were repaired in code: path normalization, Instant arithmetic and JSON parsing. Six more are gated with an ignore attribute on the Windows target until the real port lands, because they assume Unix path literals, a filesystem root of `/`, a `/var` directory, absolute `/tmp` paths and bash shell syntax. The last 2 were already deferred on macOS with the same pattern, and we extended it to Windows. The Windows job in CI now reports zero failures, so every one of the 16 cases is passing on that platform.
violating_sentence: The Windows job in CI now reports zero failures, so every one of the 16 cases is passing on that platform.
fixed_sentence: The Windows job in CI now reports zero failures, and 8 of the 16 cases are passing while 8 are skipped by the ignore gates.
why: Zero failures is read as all cases passing, but ignored tests also produce zero failures; the fix separates passing from skipped.

paragraph: The U-23 change made the path-disambiguation annotation fire on every stripped tool response, roughly 50 bytes per call across every tool except `run_command`. In real sessions inside a git worktree the repetition is loud, and the two signals the user actually wants, that the project was activated and that the session is in a worktree, are missing from the visible session state. The redesign replaces per-call emission with novelty-gated emission and adds two banners to the server instructions to carry the cold-reader signal. We replayed 40 recorded sessions through the gated emitter and saw no user complaints about missing context, so the banners are delivering the signal.
violating_sentence: We replayed 40 recorded sessions through the gated emitter and saw no user complaints about missing context, so the banners are delivering the signal.
fixed_sentence: We replayed 40 recorded sessions through the gated emitter and found both banner strings in the first server message of each, so the banners are delivering the signal.
why: Absence of complaints in replays is taken as proof the banners work, though replays have no user to complain; the fix checks the banner text is present.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: Fixed on `experiments` on 2026-07-10, together with the sibling past-cap bug. `extract_toml_key` now resolves against the fully parsed table whether or not the summary emitted `sections` or `keys`, so the dotted and flat-key fallback is always reachable, including for files that mix top-level scalars with tables. That exclusivity between branches was what made the fallback dead code before. The summary sections stay only as a fast path for precise line ranges. `extract_yaml_key` now scans uncapped top-level keys through a new helper. After the change, the false not-found reports stopped appearing in the issue queue, which confirms the YAML lookup handles every key it is given.
violating_sentence: After the change, the false not-found reports stopped appearing in the issue queue, which confirms the YAML lookup handles every key it is given.
fixed_sentence: After the change, the false not-found reports stopped appearing in the issue queue, and the new tests resolve every top-level key in the past-cap YAML fixture.
why: A quiet issue queue is treated as confirmation the lookup works, though unused or unreported paths look identical; the fix cites a test that exercised the lookup.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: Two tests cover the new status validation. The first is a create-then-read-back round trip asserting that a new bug is `open` and that a new tracker is still `draft`. That second half is the over-match guard, since a rule of "default everything to open" would pass a one-sided test and break the tracker vocabulary. The second is a refusal test for invalid values. It loops through all six documented statuses, and none of them raised the refusal error, so the validation is correctly rejecting bad input.
violating_sentence: It loops through all six documented statuses, and none of them raised the refusal error, so the validation is correctly rejecting bad input.
fixed_sentence: It loops through all six documented statuses, and none of them raised the refusal error, so the validation accepts every documented value.
why: No refusals on valid statuses cannot show invalid input is rejected, since a disabled validator is equally silent; the fix limits the claim to acceptance.
fails: banned word
shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The severity bucketing was checked against the source this week. The mapping function and its unit test were read line by line, and both agree on which kinds land in which bucket. A full-corpus run and 57 paired runs all reported the degraded flag as false. The counters disagree slightly: 47094 symbols found against 44668 bucketed repo-wide. Since the warm-up logging never printed a partial-tree message, the language servers evidently return complete symbol trees during warm-up. The single-file case shows the same gap, 44 found against 41 bucketed.
violating_sentence: Since the warm-up logging never printed a partial-tree message, the language servers evidently return complete symbol trees during warm-up.
fixed_sentence: Since the warm-up logging never printed a partial-tree message, we still do not know whether the language servers return partial symbol trees during warm-up.
why: Silence from the partial-tree log is read as proof of complete trees, though a log never wired to that branch would be equally silent; the fix reports only what is unknown.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The first candidate makes apply_ops iterate by index and, after replacing or deleting a matched key, skip that key's continuation lines. This handles every multi-line shape, because both set and delete replace the value wholesale: a nested map, a block scalar and a block sequence are all discarded the same way. The regression suite for the change passed with no failures. Since no test output mentioned orphaned continuation lines, no orphaned lines can remain after any edit. The suite does include one fixture per shape, and each was diffed against its expected file.
violating_sentence: Since no test output mentioned orphaned continuation lines, no orphaned lines can remain after any edit.
fixed_sentence: Since each fixture diff showed no orphaned continuation lines, none remain after edits to those three shapes.
why: Absence of any mention in test output is treated as proof none remain, though the tests may never check for orphans; the fix cites the diffs actually inspected and narrows scope.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The third hypothesis was that the foreign rows come from path relativization rather than being genuinely foreign. To test it, the split was counted on an independent population: 477 issue artifacts projected from a scope=all find. Of these, 451 came back relative and 26 absolute, summing exactly to the total. Relativization is therefore the discriminator, not a confound, and an absolute path in a response means the row sits outside the active project. No absolute paths turned up among the rows the earlier filter dropped, so the filter must be discarding nothing that belongs to this project.
violating_sentence: No absolute paths turned up among the rows the earlier filter dropped, so the filter must be discarding nothing that belongs to this project.
fixed_sentence: Every row the earlier filter dropped was listed, and all 26 carried absolute paths, so the filter discarded only rows outside this project.
why: Finding no absolute paths among dropped rows is used to prove the filter is harmless, though a filter that returned nothing would look the same; the fix reports the dropped rows examined.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: Closing this record reproduced the bug on itself. The call was edit_markdown with a frontmatter set for status and closed date. The file on disk flipped to fixed, yet the artifact get call kept returning open. The running server is executing an unlinked binary: /proc reports the exe as deleted, the process started at 11:10:11, and the rebuild at 11:39:59 replaced the file without touching the running image. The code answering these calls therefore predates the fix commit at 11:46:13. The server logged no errors during the edit, which shows the write path inside the running process is working correctly.
violating_sentence: The server logged no errors during the edit, which shows the write path inside the running process is working correctly.
fixed_sentence: The server logged no errors during the edit, which shows only that the stale process did not treat the write as a failure.
why: A silent error log is taken as proof the write path works, though a stale or disconnected path would also log nothing; the fix states only what silence shows.
fails: banned word
shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The default feature list in Cargo.toml includes remote-embed, http and librarian. The artifact subcommand exists only when librarian is compiled in, so a build with default features off legitimately lacks it. The CLI test builds its command through cargo_bin, which resolves the binary by path at run time and reads whatever file sits in the target directory when the test executes. It carries no record of the feature set the test binary was compiled against. Our CI job printed no missing-subcommand failures on the last run, so the artifact subcommand was present in the binary those tests exercised.
violating_sentence: Our CI job printed no missing-subcommand failures on the last run, so the artifact subcommand was present in the binary those tests exercised.
fixed_sentence: Our CI job printed no missing-subcommand failures on the last run, and its log does not say which feature set built the binary those tests exercised.
why: Lack of failures is taken as proof the subcommand was present, though tests that never ran or skipped would be equally quiet; the fix states what the log leaves open.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The create and update actions of the artifact tool paste the caller's body under the frontmatter they generate. A body that opens with its own delimited block therefore ends up holding a second frontmatter block, which the catalog never parses. We confirmed this by creating a file with such a body and running a find query on a key from the inner block: the query returned the file's generated keys only. The nightly indexer log for the affected folder shows zero parse warnings for the past week, so the indexer has evidently handled these inner blocks without trouble. Humans and agents opening the file still see the inner block and read it as authoritative.
violating_sentence: The nightly indexer log for the affected folder shows zero parse warnings for the past week, so the indexer has evidently handled these inner blocks without trouble.
fixed_sentence: The nightly indexer log for the affected folder shows zero parse warnings for the past week, but the indexer never parses inner blocks, so it could not warn about them.
why: Zero warnings is read as proof the indexer handles inner blocks, yet an indexer that ignores them would log nothing either; the fix reports the silence as expected.

paragraph: We tested two hypotheses about the doubled frontmatter. First, that the two observed instances came from hand-editing rather than a tool path. I ran the create action with a frontmatter-leading body against a live server and got the same doubled structure, so that hypothesis is rejected. Second, that only create has the seam. Running the update action with a patch of the same shape also reproduced it, so both sites need a guard. Git blame shows no commits touching those two files by a human author in the last month, which confirms that the tool alone produced every instance in the catalog.
violating_sentence: Git blame shows no commits touching those two files by a human author in the last month, which confirms that the tool alone produced every instance in the catalog.
fixed_sentence: Git blame shows no commits touching those two files by a human author in the last month, so hand-editing of those files is unlikely to explain the recent instances.
why: Absence of human commits is taken as proof of tool causation, but edits made outside git would leave the same silence; the fix narrows to what blame covers.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The report was produced while answering whether served librarian sections actually get used, a question whose answer would justify or block moving about 830 characters of tool-schema prose into served guide sections. Its headline said 100.0% never engaged. The section-view counter reads zero for every section because the counter was never wired to the serving path; a test call to a served section left it at zero. Since no section was ever viewed, section-grain serving is pure waste, and we should delete that machinery.
violating_sentence: Since no section was ever viewed, section-grain serving is pure waste, and we should delete that machinery.
fixed_sentence: Since the counter never registers views, usage of section-grain serving is unmeasured, and we should not delete that machinery yet.
why: Zero views is treated as proof of no use, though the paragraph shows the counter is disconnected and would read zero regardless; the fix states it is unmeasured.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The actual seam is the adapter's call method, the one place that receives both the core tool context, with its agent field, and the raw input JSON carrying the action string. The guard now runs there, gated on the inner tool's name being doc and on a new classifier covering exactly the ten mutating actions this bug named. The seven read actions are exempt, and tests assert each of them passes through ungated. After deploying to the staging server we saw no rejected calls in the logs over a day of traffic, so the guard is clearly enforcing correctly for agents without the field.
violating_sentence: After deploying to the staging server we saw no rejected calls in the logs over a day of traffic, so the guard is clearly enforcing correctly for agents without the field.
fixed_sentence: After deploying to the staging server we saw no rejected calls in the logs over a day of traffic, and no agent without the field sent a mutating call in that window.
why: No rejections is read as proof the guard enforces, yet a disabled guard would also reject nothing; the fix reports the absence as only reflecting traffic.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The markdown edit module gains a constant listing the five section-edit actions, plus a function that checks the action is dispatchable. It is called at all three dispatchers right after the action is read and before the edit branch. The three missing-action hints now render from the same constant, so the two paths at each site cannot drift. The section-edit planner's own four-member message is untouched. A grep for the old hard-coded action lists across the source tree returned nothing, so the new check must be firing on every malformed call.
violating_sentence: A grep for the old hard-coded action lists across the source tree returned nothing, so the new check must be firing on every malformed call.
fixed_sentence: A grep for the old hard-coded action lists across the source tree returned nothing, so no dispatcher still carries its own copy of the list.
why: An empty grep is taken as proof the check fires on malformed calls, but it only shows lists are gone; the fix claims just that.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: The handoff on the id-citation scan is short. The scan is a plain substring search over tracked files, so any file quoting the sixteen-character id is listed, and the response test asserts that shape for both a hit and a miss. Fields the caller did not ask about come back as null instead of an empty list. I ran the scan from a shallow worktree whose index had not been refreshed since the move. For the renamed tracker note, the scan handed back an empty list, so no other file still cites its old id. The next step is to rerun it from the main checkout.
violating_sentence: For the renamed tracker note, the scan handed back an empty list, so no other file still cites its old id.
fixed_sentence: For the renamed tracker note, the scan handed back an empty list, so it listed no citer of the old id in that worktree.
why: An empty list from a scan run on a stale index is what a dead scan also returns, so it cannot prove no citers exist; the fix scopes the claim to what was listed.

paragraph: The shrink guard stayed silent on all forty replacements in the batch, so it is catching shrinkage properly. It runs immediately before the splice and compares the replaced lines with the new body, never the whole file. Its advisory is joined onto the existing warning key instead of overwriting it, and the thirty existing replace tests pass unchanged, which shows the lone-warning output is byte-identical. The batch itself was pushed through the dry-run path, which returns before the guard is ever called.
violating_sentence: The shrink guard stayed silent on all forty replacements in the batch, so it is catching shrinkage properly.
fixed_sentence: The shrink guard stayed silent on all forty replacements in the batch, and each new body kept at least the old line count.
why: Silence from a guard that the dry-run path never calls is indistinguishable from a working guard; the fix reports the line counts actually compared instead of inferring correctness.

paragraph: The size check subtracts each prompt surface's byte length from its cap. On two of the three surfaces the gap was close to zero when I measured, so edits there must be net-neutral or measured first. The third surface never produced a size warning in CI this week, so it has plenty of headroom. Nobody has recorded the byte figures, because they shift on every prompt-surface commit and would go stale the same day. The CI job that emits size warnings was switched off during the runner migration and came back only on Friday.
violating_sentence: The third surface never produced a size warning in CI this week, so it has plenty of headroom.
fixed_sentence: The third surface never produced a size warning in CI this week, and its margin has not been measured.
why: No warnings is what a switched-off CI job also produces, so it cannot show headroom; the fix reports the silence as silence and admits the margin is unmeasured.

paragraph: The stale description of those two lines was challenged by reading the working tree, which held another session's uncommitted hoist that had already moved them. The live file gave a confident answer that described work in flight, not the original. Reading the committed version separates the two, and the indent width, four spaces against eight, survives as the tell. That other session's delete edit had specified the eight-space block and succeeded, which it could not have done had the code already been hoisted. I ran the history search against the pre-move path of the module. The history search returned zero commits touching those lines, so nobody has edited them since the handoff.
violating_sentence: The history search returned zero commits touching those lines, so nobody has edited them since the handoff.
fixed_sentence: The history search returned zero commits touching those lines under the pre-move path, which excludes only that path.
why: Zero hits from a search on a path that no longer holds the file is what nobody-edited would also give; the fix states what the search covered.
fails: shares an 8-token shingle with its seed

paragraph: This case put the mutation in output.rs and the test in tests.rs. Two of the day's runs kept the test inside the mutated file, and there the test went red the moment the mutation landed, which shows those two were sound. The cross-file run stayed green with zero failures after the mutation, so its test is sound as well. Committing the test first costs one commit on every run, so the cost is better billed only to cross-file cases, one run in three here.
violating_sentence: The cross-file run stayed green with zero failures after the mutation, so its test is sound as well.
fixed_sentence: The cross-file run stayed green with zero failures after the mutation, so its test never reacted to it.
why: Zero failures after a mutation is exactly what a test that never touches the mutated code produces; the fix reads the green run as non-reaction, not soundness.

paragraph: The lock check before a gate run on the shared checkout kept reporting that the machine was free, and I traced why. The check matches on process name with an exact-match flag, so it sees only real cargo processes; running it while a gate was live returned that process's PID, which confirms it can return a hit. The nightly harness is a different case: it can outlive its cargo parent, and the name match cannot see it. On three consecutive mornings the name match printed nothing, so no harness process was left over from the night before. I then killed the shared runner by hand for a second-order cleanup, and the checkout stayed clean afterward.
violating_sentence: On three consecutive mornings the name match printed nothing, so no harness process was left over from the night before.
fixed_sentence: On three consecutive mornings the name match printed nothing, and a scan of the deps directory path found no leftover harness process either.
why: Empty output from a name match proves nothing when the harness can outlive cargo and be invisible to it; the fix reports a check that could see the harness.

paragraph: The recorder table has a coverage gap that is separate from the ordering bug described here. Native shell calls from the arm under evaluation leave no row, and I confirmed this by running a marker command through that arm and diffing the table before and after: the row count did not change. The timestamps are a different matter. Each row's called_at is the completion instant, and subtracting latency_ms recovers the start, which I checked against three calls timed by hand. The ordering complaint therefore concerns only calls that are recorded. Since the table shows no rows for native shell calls in the last week, the arm has not been running any shell commands.
violating_sentence: Since the table shows no rows for native shell calls in the last week, the arm has not been running any shell commands.
fixed_sentence: Since the table shows no rows for native shell calls in the last week, the arm's shell usage in that week is unknown, because the recorder cannot see them.
why: The paragraph itself says native shell calls leave no row, so empty rows are what a blind recorder produces; the fix states that the silence is uninformative.

paragraph: Two settings structs now carry the embedding configuration, and they have drifted. The global section is already four fields behind the project section, which a field-by-field diff of the two definitions shows. Bug aae547c917c329b5 came from a second embedder reading the environment inside its own constructor, and I reproduced it by setting a different value in the process environment and watching the constructor ignore the loaded config. The startup dotenv loader logged no warnings when the machine value overrode the project value, so the override path is working as intended. Adding a new setting today means editing both structs.
violating_sentence: The startup dotenv loader logged no warnings when the machine value overrode the project value, so the override path is working as intended.
fixed_sentence: The startup dotenv loader logged no warnings when the machine value overrode the project value, and the resolved config dump showed the machine value winning.
why: A silent log is also what a loader with no warning code would produce; the fix cites the resolved config as direct evidence instead of silence.

paragraph: Source pins for the survey are recorded below so a later reader can re-run the comparison. The evals repository was read at tip 339779f from 2026-08-19, and the gauntlet repository at tip 91b6f7e from 2026-08-06; section 6 draws only on the second. I searched the serf checkout for uses of the word evener with a recursive grep and got zero matches outside the about file, so the project does not use that name anywhere in its behavior. The obol repository was pinned at its v0.9.0 tag, which I confirmed by checking out the tag and comparing the commit hash.
violating_sentence: I searched the serf checkout for uses of the word evener with a recursive grep and got zero matches outside the about file, so the project does not use that name anywhere in its behavior.
fixed_sentence: I searched the serf checkout for uses of the word evener with a recursive grep and got zero matches outside the about file, so no source file or config there spells that name.
why: Zero grep matches show only that the string is absent from files, not from runtime behavior; the fix narrows the claim to what grep covered.

paragraph: The symbol-editing tools have a few extent problems worth recording. The read path for find_symbol with bodies uses raw LSP ranges, while the write tools apply assorted trims, so an agent sees a different body extent than replace_symbol would overwrite; I showed this by comparing the two ranges on a function with a leading attribute. The declaration-line helper only knows Rust prefixes. It never matches on a Python def or a Go func line. The clamp to the closing brace introduced BUG-016 when it was added to address BUG-014. The panic test suite passes with no failures on the const-item fixtures, so const items are safe from that corruption now.
violating_sentence: The panic test suite passes with no failures on the const-item fixtures, so const items are safe from that corruption now.
fixed_sentence: The panic test suite passes with no failures on the const-item fixtures, and its assertions compare each const item's file bytes before and after the edit.
why: A passing suite proves safety only if it can fail on this corruption; the fix states what the tests actually checked.

paragraph: Review notes on the guide index refactor. The `heading.clone()` call re-allocates about fifteen short strings per guide, which we measured with a counting allocator over the full guide set. The module doc for the index file never describes the build and lookup surface, so a new reader has to open the tests to learn it. The ceiling's panic message reports the raw compiled-in body length instead of the on-the-wire cost, and we confirmed that by reading the assertion. The test-only adapter helper depends on tool registration order, and the duplicated doc rationale sits in two path-naming helpers. The dead-code lint printed nothing on the new module, so the helper functions are all reachable from production callers.
violating_sentence: The dead-code lint printed nothing on the new module, so the helper functions are all reachable from production callers.
fixed_sentence: The dead-code lint printed nothing on the new module, so no helper is flagged unused, though tests alone could be keeping some alive.
why: Lint silence is treated as proof of production reachability, but test callers or a suppressed lint would produce the same silence; the fix reports only what the lint showed.

paragraph: Handoff on tool routing after last week's eval. We reviewed 40 agent transcripts from the run. Symbol overviews now go through the symbols tool, and bodies through the same tool with the body flag; in every transcript that touched source, at least one such call appears. The shell tool is reserved for tests, git and build steps. The audit log for the shell tool shows zero source-reading commands across all 40 runs, so the tool description steering agents away from raw grep is working. Edits split between the structural editor for code and the text editor for everything else, and new files always use the write tool.
violating_sentence: The audit log for the shell tool shows zero source-reading commands across all 40 runs, so the tool description steering agents away from raw grep is working.
fixed_sentence: The audit log for the shell tool shows zero source-reading commands across all 40 runs, so agents in this sample did not read source through the shell.
why: Zero shell reads is attributed to the tool description working, but agents that never tried the shell would show the same zero; the fix states only the observed absence.

paragraph: The miss is returned as a downcastable typed error carrying tier, heading, diagnostic and a base hint. Its Display output joins the diagnostic and the hint, so the markdown editor shows the full message with no extra work. The body-edit routine downcasts the error and, only when it holds an augmented artifact and the tier is visible drift, appends the params nudge. Callers without that context just print the Display text. After the change, the integration log contained no reports of a missing nudge, so the downcast path is delivering the nudge correctly in production.
violating_sentence: After the change, the integration log contained no reports of a missing nudge, so the downcast path is delivering the nudge correctly in production.
fixed_sentence: After the change, the integration log contained no reports of a missing nudge, and the unit test for the downcast path shows the nudge appended.

paragraph: One real client does send per-request conversation metadata, contradicting the earlier claim that none does: the OpenAI Codex CLI merged a turn-metadata key inside `_meta` in March. Because the key is vendor-namespaced, the eventual shape of rank 3 is a probe list of known keys, much like the session-variable list at rank 2. Claude Code and Claude Desktop send no conversation identifier, which an open first-party issue confirms. Our proxy capture of claude.ai traffic contained no metadata field at all, so the web client must be stripping it before the request leaves the browser.

fixed_sentence: Our proxy capture of claude.ai traffic contained no metadata field at all, so that client sends none in the captured requests.

paragraph: Layer 4 shipped in August. The context action now detects an entry-grain anchor and returns before the file-grain capped-candidates path, serving the anchor statement plus the statements on either side. Neighbours are deduplicated by reference, not by edge, so an artifact that both cites and is cited by the anchor appears once as mutual. Ordering runs mutual, then cited-by, then cites, then lexicographic, which the two-pass packing tests assert. The overflow block came back with an empty unresolved-edges list on every anchor we queried, so the edge resolver is finding every citation target.

fixed_sentence: The overflow block came back with an empty unresolved-edges list on every anchor we queried, so no anchor reported a dangling citation.

paragraph: The routing review for the profile loader ran on 2026-08-28. So the test spawns sync against a slow store that is provably in flight and probes from outside at 100ms. As I remember it, the suite passes 42 of 42 with the binding changed to a bare underscore, which is why this probe test matters. Without it, that regression would ship silently.

paragraph: The path extractor had a polarity defect. Capitalization is the discriminator, since Type/method and mcpServers/codescout/env all carry uppercase while real directory names here are lowercase. The resolver had a separate gap: resolve_file_line never had the basename fallback that resolve_file_path has, so process.rs:66-135 was reported missing at high severity even though the reference is valid. paragraph: The pipeline tests cover six cases. In the happy path, the three-stage command `seq 1 100 | grep ^5 | wc -l` yields 11: the single "5", the ten values 50 through 59. For pipefail, stage 1 returns non-zero, stage 2 never runs, and the result carries `stopped_at: 1` with only two stage entries. Stdin wiring is checked so that each stage receives exactly the previous stage's stdout, with no leakage or doubling. A dangerous stage is rejected before any stage starts. As the spec describes it, the timeout applies per stage, so a two-second limit lets each of `sleep 5` and `cat` run separately. The last case pairs a pipeline with background mode and expects a recoverable error.

The leading hypothesis is that the rename-over-target step is invisible to the file watcher's Windows backend. No isolated A/B test toggled the write path, so this stays deferred. Next step is a minimal script that writes one file both ways under the watcher and logs the events it receives.

Beside the earlier run on the other config file, where the same edit shape applied both halves, the defect is layer-specific: the top-level env block drops deletions on /mcp, and the per-server env block does not. So adding one declaration flips the entire topic. Every other tool that routes to that topic will drop to preamble only until it gains its own declaration, so I listed those tools in the handoff.

paragraph: Two sessions touched the same config file this week, and one commit swept up the other's half-finished edits. The interleaving is the problem: `git add -p` cannot separate the hunks because the edits sit inside one block. Checking the diff right before committing only narrows the window rather than closing it. The remedy on offer is social: do not commit a path another session is known to be working, and report rather than repair when you find you have. Afterwards I ran the full test suite on the swept-up commit and it passed, so the peer's edits were evidently safe to have committed. That is policy, not mechanism, and is recorded as such.

why: A passing suite says nothing about whether committing another session's in-progress edits was safe or intended. The fix states what the green run does show.

Since every commit carries a `Session-Id` trailer, every author in these stacks has been cleared to merge. The ladder needs each author cleared, not just named, so the gate should read the clearance list directly.

A namespace at top level is also wrapped in an expression statement. Running the extractor on a file whose only top-level item was an abstract class returned an empty symbol list, and the same happened for a lone namespace. After adding the two arms, the crate compiles cleanly, so namespaces and abstract classes now show up with all their members in the symbol tree.

paragraph: The references tool resolves the symbol position in the definition file and then asks the language client for references. That client opens only the definition file before sending the request. It never syncs the caller files, and it does not wait for the server to finish loading the project after a reindex. Right after an incremental reindex the server has not yet loaded the recently changed callers, so it returns just the definition and we report zero external callers. To check the symbol is unused, we ran references on it once, got zero external callers, and concluded nothing else in the repo calls it.

why: The references tool can return a false zero after reindex, so it does not measure whether callers exist; the fix uses a text search that does.

That drift is real, since a diff of the two files shows different content in the first twenty lines. Until the two paths are merged, someone has to hand-copy changes between the files after each onboarding run.

paragraph: The line-start proposal was dropped after a probe run. The guard that protects against splicing a new function into an unrelated body depends on matching exactly those lines. The comment-skipping option is cheaper, because leading `//` and `#` lines are already skipped. The alternative also narrows matches in the safe direction, since it removes only text that is provably not code. We ran the Python fixture suite against the line-start version and it passed, so the line-start check is safe for the Rust definitions the guard protects.

paragraph: The embeddings migration runs in a fixed order. The old table is then renamed with a v1 suffix, a vec0 virtual table is created at the recorded dimension, rows are copied across, and the old table is dropped. I ran the migration against a fresh test database and it exited with status zero, which confirms that existing rows keep their embeddings and remain searchable afterward. paragraph: The edit planner depends only on the existing trailing-newline normalizer. Each PlannedEdit carries a span, a replacement, its edit index, and an order value. The overlap detector returns a recoverable error naming both conflicting edit indexes. Non-empty spans conflict when their half-open ranges intersect, and a zero-width insert conflicts only when it lies strictly inside a non-empty span. Two zero-width inserts never conflict, and at equal offsets they land in ascending order. The applier splices from the end backward, then normalizes the newline once. Type checking passed on the new module, so the overlap detector returns an error for every pair of intersecting spans.

why: Type checking does not test overlap detection behaviour on intersecting spans. The fix claims only signature agreement, which the check measured.

paragraph: The append-at-end path for the last section produced a stray blank line in the new byte-splice editor. Legacy code joins the lines before the insertion point and always adds a newline, so when the insertion index equals the line count the joined prefix is the content plus one extra newline. Our splice version copies the raw bytes instead, so it lacks that newline. We added a leading newline to the replacement for that single case. The splice output now matches legacy for the last-section case, because the whole suite compiles and passes on the branch. Every other edit arm has its boundary strictly below the line count, so it needs no special handling.

paragraph: Scoped npm packages needed a naming decision before auto-registration could ship. The registry name is @scope/name, but the scope lookup syntax uses a colon-delimited key where a slash would be ambiguous. We normalize the slash to a double underscore, so @babel/core becomes lib:@babel__core, while the original name stays in the entry metadata for display. Language detection is simple: a tsconfig file in the package directory means typescript, otherwise javascript. There are no search_pattern hints for cache paths, because auto-registration puts dependencies into list_libraries and agents then use a lib-prefixed scope. paragraph: Several risks remain for the end_line clamp. Python parents are indentation-based, and tree-sitter-python reports a class end_line as its last body line, so the clamp is still sound but needs Python-specific assertions. For C# partial classes, find_parent_symbol looks only in the current file's tree, which is correct because cross-file partials are structurally separate parents. For Go, the clamp is a no-op since methods have no structural parent in DocumentSymbol. Java and Kotlin cold starts take 30 to 60 seconds, so the suites share one LSP and cap at five minutes. paragraph: The edit tool will match on whitespace-normalized text, gated on uniqueness. A linter or AST check catches grammar breakage but cannot see an edit that lands in a wrong-but-still-parsing location, which is the failure relaxation introduces. Safety therefore has to come from the match being unique. Normalization is conservative: per-line leading and trailing whitespace plus line endings, nothing internal. A curly-quote miss still falls through to the nearest-text error. We ran the relaxed matcher over 200 recorded edits and the linter reported zero syntax errors, so no edit landed in the wrong place. Batch edits are deferred.

When the fallback is suppressed, the arm returns the existing recoverable error with its hint, keeping the lock-holder lookup and retry guidance. The rare case where the replacement intentionally carries an escaped quote is caught by the existing verify-the-result note. Decoding is limited to escaped double and single quotes, never doubled backslashes, because those appear in regex literals and Windows paths. After a bump every rule counts as unseen, so the next matching tool call or user turn surfaces it again. We ran the hook against a scratch session and the epoch counter went from 0 to 1 to 2 across two forced compactions. The rules therefore re-appear in the model's context after compaction, which is what users need. We did not build on PreCompact injecting content directly, because its payload is unverified; the design leans on the two channels already known to work.

Reads are different: a normalized match there is harmless. We also do not detect or block edits to rendered regions such as the State section, though we surface a hint toward params when the failure signature fits. The hint logic passed all twelve unit tests on the failure-signature matcher, which confirms that users who hit this failure now switch to params instead of retrying body edits. The session-start script runs on every source, lists that directory, picks entries whose ppid is on its own ancestry, and writes the current session id into the match. The server notices the update by comparing the file's mtime on each call, which costs one fstat and no parse. Stale entries from dead servers are ignored because their ppid is not in the ancestry.

paragraph: When a refutation arrives, the tap closes the valid-time interval by setting valid_until to the best estimate of when the claim stopped holding, and recorded_at to now. It does not default valid_until to now, because the tap discovers the closure rather than causing it. The statement is then routed to the same worklist that fired condition events reach, so it is no longer served as fact. The prose is left untouched: the record of what was believed and when is the asset, and post-mortems ask exactly that. Our replay of forty refuted statements showed every one with a closed interval, so none of them is still being served as fact.

paragraph: We compared four options for the audit trail. A Rust-layer wrapper sees rich identity but cannot see out-of-band writers, so every forgotten call site is a standing gap. Full images on every op would multiply reindex churn against 1 KB artifact rows for no forensic gain over diffs. Age-based pruning is safe for old entries, since the pruning job exited zero on last week's copy of the table. Git cannot carry the in-transaction guarantee, because commits land only after the transaction closes, so it stays a replica only.

paragraph: Concurrent event creation on one artifact produced a fan of parent edges instead of a chain. Each call read the latest event before either had written, so both picked the same parent. The registry now holds one mutex per artifact id, taken after payload validation and held until the transaction commits. On my laptop the directory holds 212 files after six days, which matches roughly 35 starts a day. Nothing prunes the directory, so the count only climbs, and a week of CI runs on a shared runner would add several hundred more. The reader loads every file in the directory once at startup, and that path stays cheap at a thousand files, since the CI job that loads a single ledger file finishes green.

paragraph: The split of the tools module follows a fixed order. First, survey the module's symbols to get a full inventory before splitting. Then categorize every symbol into types, params, guards or other. Extract the types file first, since the others import from it, then params, which has no dependency on guards, then guards. Move the tests into their own file and widen private helpers to crate visibility where the tests use them. Write thin re-export modules at the core and outer levels. paragraph: The substitution is the interesting part, not the bug. Comparing start time against build time is a proxy for an event the script cannot observe, namely whether this process loaded the current bytes, and it errs in both directions: a process started between the build finishing and the rename completing reads fresh and is not, while a rebuild producing identical bytes reads stale and is not. The deleted marker is not a comparison at all; it is the kernel reporting that the inode the process holds is no longer the one at that path. From the proc filesystem documentation alone, listing the process's executable link prints the path with a deleted suffix, though nobody has run that here. The remedy takes the signal from the event's own side of the boundary.

paragraph: The batch edit bug is an intra-call ordering flaw, not a concurrency problem. Every mutating call already runs under the write guard, which holds an in-process mutex and a cross-process file lock for the whole call, and the failing batch reproduces with a single client, so no second writer is involved. Reading the guard's source, I see that a second process calling acquire while the lock is held returns an immediate error with a busy status instead of waiting. That is why a queue would add cost without curing this defect. The proposed fix resolves headings against a snapshot taken before any edit is applied, which makes the result independent of edit order.

paragraph: Each symbol lookup may trigger a document-open for every file visited, and the LSP mux fans these out per client tag. If the document state keeps content blobs without bounded eviction, repeated visits across thousands of files would accumulate linearly. Taking 50 KB per stored file, 60 GB of resident memory works out to about 1.2M stored documents, which is plausible for a long-running session that touches a Kotlin monorepo. The eviction code has no size cap: the store is a plain map and the only removal path is the explicit close call. Currently there are 340 open sessions holding documents, so the leak is widespread.

The 300 s idle timeout stops the JVM but leaves the index directory intact. Nothing else on the host writes analyzer data, so cleanup has to come from this component. paragraph: Reviewing the start path turned up a duplicate-spawn race. When a start fails, each waiter in get_or_start wakes on the watch value Some(false), registers a fresh starting channel, and calls do_start, so one key can spawn several LSP processes. The cleanup guard's drop removes the starting entry unconditionally, which also removes the barrier for late arrivals. Nothing else in the manager touches that entry, so no other code path can restore the barrier. The extra processes are terminated when their Arc drops, so the effect is transient rather than a permanent leak. It shows up only when a first start overlaps a transient failure.

A grep for `max_lines` in the test directory turned up two hits, both in fixtures for the exploring mode. Every truncation path in the reader is therefore covered by that one line-count check. If the shape allows the case but the values never produce it, reading proves nothing, and only a run shows it. For the wrapping patch I disabled the change and ran the tests sharing the phrase `wrap_long` through a name filter instead of running one test alone. Each of the three went red. Three red results under the `wrap_long` filter show every test in the suite exercises the patched path.

why: The name filter selected three tests, but the sentence generalizes to every test in the suite; the fix names the filtered tests only.

paragraph: The negative result carried an explicit do-not-repeat note, and it still lapsed within four days. The decay was a stale warning, not a stale fact, so no freshness check would flag it. paragraph: Grepping the moved basenames under tools/ turned up no stale citations, so every live surface is clean after the 24 moves. paragraph: Handoff note on the ledger prefix work. The catalog lives in a machine-local SQLite file that is git-ignored, so a fresh clone starts with no declarations and the allocator has nothing to read for them. Reservations are different: the allocator re-derives the maximum from the committed body, so those survive a clone. To size the exposure I ran a query on my profile for rows whose declaration column was non-empty and whose ledger name began with `HY`. It returned 54 rows, so every declaration in the catalog exists only in this one file. I therefore propose moving the prefix into frontmatter, which is committed, so a ledger's identity travels with the repo instead of one profile's database.

paragraph: Notes from the backlog sweep. Readers land on the section form of each item, because `artifact(get)` returns the section and the table sits far below under an older dated heading that makes it look stale. That is why the verify-open pass ran against sections. To check the pass, I grepped the section text for the `**Status:**` marker with the value `open` and read every hit. Twelve items matched, and each one had a table row still marked open, so all open items in the backlog are confirmed open. BL-45 was in the hit list, and its table row said `done`, shipped at a named commit with five tests, so I am correcting that entry before any report carries it.
